Issued at 253 AM EST Wed Nov 4 2026

At 245am EST Wednesday morning, a large upper level trough was 
spinning over the Midwest, with its associated 1000mb surface low 
positioned along the IA/MN border. Ahead of this low, deep southerly 
flow is pulling rich Gulf moisture northward across the Ohio Valley 
and Great Lakes Regions, with PW values of 1.5-1.8 inches along and 
west of the I-65 corridor in Kentucky and southern Indiana. As this 
low lifts north into the Upper Midwest today, its attendant cold 
front will gradually traverse the local area. Ahead of this front, 
gusty winds and heavy rainfall are concerns; behind it, winds will 
ease and rain come to an end, though clouds will linger the 
remainder of the day.

*** GUSTY WIND POTENTIAL ***

Scattered showers were percolating across the area as a low level 
jet (LLJ) promotes isentropic upglide. A somewhat stable planetary 
boundary layer (PBL) should in general limit the transfer of 
momentum from the 50-55 kt winds clocked on KLVX's vad at 1km (~3200 
ft) AGL, though sporadic gusts to 30+ mph (recently observed at SDF) 
may continue through dawn. Thereafter, various REFS members suggest 
a heavier band of showers will develop along the eastward-meandering 
cold front. REFS ensemble mean brings gusts to 30-40 mph with this 
wave of rain, and even gives 15-30% (highest south) chances for 
gusts over 40 mph between roughly the I-65 and I-75 corridors in 
Kentucky during the 8am to noon EST timeframe. It would make 
meteorological sense that this would be our best opportunity for 
those stronger wind gusts, as (1) winds aloft will remain strong 
during this time and (2) these heavier showers will feature the 
strongest downdrafts. Still, given widespread clouds and rain 
showers, low levels are forecast to remain somewhat stable, limiting 
mixing on the whole and keeping the coverage and duration of those 
stronger gusts low.

*** HEAVY RAIN POTENTIAL ***

In addition to gusty winds, widespread rainfall ahead of the front 
today should benefit the ongoing drought. The near-record PW values 
approaching 1.8 inches coupled with a 10-12 kft deep warm cloud 
layer suggests showers ahead of the front will be efficient rain 
producers with hourly rates approaching an inch at times. In 
addition, the orientation of mean cloud layer winds nearly parallel 
to the (slow-moving) cold front suggests training of heavier 
showers, which could allow some locations to see 3+ inches of 
rainfall in just a 6 hour period. REFS LPMM suggests this is most 
likely along and west of roughly the I-65 corridor, especially south 
of E-town where NBM maintains 10-30% probabilities (for 3+ inches). 
This would imply a nonzero (but still low) risk for flooding in 
urban and poor drainage areas, especially if any leaves clog storm 
drains. However, most locations are expected to see between 1 and 2 
inches of rainfall, which is much needed.

The cold front will bring an end to the rain and gusty winds from 
west to east today, reaching I-65 around 1-2pm and the I-75 corridor 
around 5-6pm EST. Behind it, however, we'll hang onto clouds and may 
even see some patchy drizzle this evening into tonight.

*** EXTENDED PERIOD ***

Conditions will turn drier on Thursday and we may even see some 
breaks of sunshine during the afternoon ahead of the next shortwave 
trough which will pass through the Lower Great Lakes on Friday. The 
LREF suggests a 40-70% probability 850mb temps drop to sub 0 degC 
near and north of an Owensboro to Richmond line Friday into 
Saturday, which indicates our area will be cool to kick off the 
weekend. In fact, forecast highs are in the mid 50s for Saturday - 
much more seasonable for early November. Clouds Friday night should 
keep lows from falling too far, but Saturday night we may see some 
frost or even localized freezing conditions (particularly over the 
Bluegrass) as clear skies and light winds make for efficient 
radiational cooling. Continued northwest flow will maintain dry and 
seasonably cool conditions into early Monday, with a gradual warming 
trend next work week.
